unit.name: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services (Botany)

chapter: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services
question_text: Enumerate the morphological adaptations of hydrophytes.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 13, book p.36, SAQ 3. All six of the book's points are kept and grouped into four marked blocks; the examples (Wolffia, Eichhornia, Vallisneria, Nymphaea) are added from standard texts because the book gives none for this question. Morphological means the features visible from outside — root, stem, leaf — which is how the blocks are ordered. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun. The 1+1+1+1 split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services · 4 marks

steps.label: Root system
lines: Root system is poorly developed, and in
some plants it is absent (Wolffia).
The roots are mostly adventitious, short
and fibrous.
They fix the plant to the mud rather than
absorb water.
steps.why: The main job of a root is to absorb water. A hydrophyte absorbs water over its whole surface, so the root is left with only the fixing job and stays small.
common_mistakes: Writing that hydrophytes have a well developed tap root. The root system is poorly developed and adventitious.
Saying roots are absent in all hydrophytes. They are absent only in a few, such as Wolffia.
steps.memory_tip: The root fixes the plant; it does not absorb the water. That one sentence gives the whole block.
steps.margin_note: Four blocks for four marks. Root, root cap, stem, leaf — in that order.

steps.label: Root caps and root pockets
lines: Root caps are absent.
In their place root pockets are present.
A root pocket is a loose sheath that covers
the root tip in water, but it does not grow
along with the tip as a root cap does.
Ex: Eichhornia, Pistia.
steps.why: A root cap protects the tip against hard soil particles. In water there is nothing to rub against, so the cap is replaced by the simpler root pocket.
common_mistakes: Writing root pouch or root cover. The term marked is root pocket.
Saying root caps are present but small. They are absent.
steps.memory_tip: No soil to scrape past, so no cap — just a pocket.
steps.margin_note: This is a named-term block. The words root pocket are the mark.

steps.label: Stem
lines: Stems are long, slender, flexible and
spongy, so moving water bends them
instead of breaking them.
In rooted hydrophytes the stem is a rhizome
buried in the mud.
In free floating forms it is short and
stoloniferous.
steps.why: A hydrophyte stem is not a supporting pillar, because water already holds the plant up. It only has to survive being bent, so it is flexible instead of woody.
common_mistakes: Writing that the stem is hard and woody. That is a xerophyte stem.
Leaving out the word flexible, which is the key term for this block.
steps.memory_tip: Water holds it up, current bends it — so slender and flexible, never woody.
steps.margin_note: Two lines are enough. Keep the word flexible in the first one.

steps.label: Leaves

lines.text: Submerged leaves thin; floating leaves waxy

lines: Submerged leaves are thin, long and ribbon
shaped or linear, and in some plants finely
dissected. Ex: Vallisneria, Ceratophyllum.
Floating leaves are large and flat, with a
waxy coating on the upper surface and a
long petiole. Ex: Nymphaea, Nelumbo.
steps.why: The two leaf forms answer two different problems: a submerged leaf must let gases and light through thin tissue, while a floating leaf must stay dry on top, which the wax provides.
common_mistakes: Describing only one leaf type. Both the submerged and the floating form are marked.
Putting the waxy coating on the lower surface. The wax is on the upper surface, the side exposed to air.
steps.memory_tip: Under water: thin and ribbon shaped. On the surface: broad and waxy on top.
steps.margin_note: This block carries two contrasting forms, so give one example on each side.

insider_note: Morphological means what is visible from outside, so keep aerenchyma and cuticle out of this answer — those are anatomical adaptations and earn nothing here.
